scenes.title: What are we delegating?
scenes.body:
Generative AI produces text, images, code, and other outputs. An agentic workflow connects that generation to tools, memory, and actions.

Drafting an email, finding a source, and changing an account cross different boundaries of authority.

Evaluate the whole workflow: what it can do, what it knows, and what happens when it is wrong.
scenes.visual:
A conceptual progression

  1. GeneratePropose an answer
  2. RetrieveBring evidence into context
  3. ActChange something outside the conversation

More authority calls for stronger checks at the boundary.
scenes.notes: Ask the room for one task they already delegate. Distinguish a model from the application wrapped around it. This progression is a teaching model, not a historical law.

scenes.title: Start with the work we want to improve.
scenes.body:
Before looking at examples, I want to set out the questions I bring to any AI-assisted workflow, including my own.

Define the tasks, agree on what better work looks like, and assess quality, productivity, and cost together. Distinguish expected benefits from observed results and causal evidence.

Build in task-specific evaluation, review, and a clear path to escalate problems and correct outcomes.
scenes.visual:
Shared design questions

Useful capability
Which tasks, and what comparison establishes improvement?
Sustainable results
How will we track quality, failure rates, time, and cost?
Human accountability
What can a reviewer inspect, stop, or reverse?
Learning from problems
How can people raise concerns, contest outcomes, and record corrections?

A framework for organizational adoption and my personal workbench.
scenes.notes: Introduce these as shared design questions before the industry overview and company example. Apply them to the speaker’s own work as well as organizational adoption. Task-specific comparisons, failure rates, escalation records, and routes to contest or correct outcomes make improvement assessable. Distinguish modeled benefits, observed changes, and causal evidence. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not findings about any company. Keep this preface constructive: the aim is to help people deliver useful work sustainably and learn from problems.

scenes.title: Private-sector adoption is uneven.
scenes.body:
U.S. Census data show 17–20% of businesses reporting AI use from December 2025 to May 2026. This covers AI broadly, across business functions.

Among firms with 250 or more employees, 37% reported using AI. Adoption varies by company size and sector.

Using AI, integrating it into workflows, and demonstrating better outcomes are separate milestones.
scenes.visual:
Business adoption · Census, May 2026 report

17–20%Businesses reporting AI use
Across the Dec 2025–May 2026 period
37%Firms with 250 or more employees
Reporting AI use

AI in any business function. These figures include more than generative AI and do not measure deployment quality.
scenes.notes: Scope confirmed by the speaker: private-sector adoption. Distinguish individual use, company integration, and demonstrated outcomes. Census changed question wording in November 2025; do not present this as an uninterrupted growth series or a GenAI-only adoption rate. The overall range spans the reporting period; the large-firm figure is the report’s size-group example.

scenes.title: The developer’s work is shifting.
scenes.body:
I work at a company pursuing broad internal AI adoption. Management is looking for greater productivity and higher quality in software production.

Development is shifting toward a person directing an AI assistant to do the coding, then applying domain expertise to review the workflow and the product it produces.

Keeping generative-AI costs contained is part of the challenge.

Firsthand experience · management goals, not measured outcomes
scenes.visual:
The changing development workflow

  1. Person: define the task and domain needs
  2. AI assistant: implement the code
  3. Person: review workflow and product
  4. Direct revisions and check the result

The assistant’s coding role grows; domain judgment and review remain human responsibilities.
scenes.notes: This section paraphrases the speaker’s supplied firsthand account of broad internal AI adoption. Keep the employer unnamed in this account and distinguish personal experience from measured adoption outcomes. Higher productivity and quality are management objectives, not measured gains reported by the speaker. The workflow is shifting; do not imply that every developer or task already follows it or that the employer endorses this presentation.

scenes.kicker: 05 · The connection to my own work
scenes.title: The same concerns recur at work and at home.
scenes.body:
Some of the issues I have been working through personally are also concerns in the organization: accuracy with efficiency, accountability of results, and making knowledge durable.

These connect the internal-adoption discussion to my own work on explicit policies, reviewable evidence, and governed memory.

Discussion question: how do we improve the work while containing cost and preserving responsibility for the result?
scenes.visual:
Shared concerns

Accuracy with efficiency
Useful progress that survives review
Accountability
Results someone can inspect and own
Durable knowledge
Context that outlives the session
Cost containment
AI use within a sustainable budget
scenes.notes: Use this as the transition into the personal workbench. The overlap is in the problems being addressed; it does not imply the employer uses ClaimWright, GroundRecall, or the other personal repositories. For discussion, consider model usage cost alongside human review and rework; this is a proposed evaluation lens, not a reported company accounting practice. Do not invent expenditure figures, savings, or an achieved productivity multiplier.

scenes.title: Make scientific virtues operational.
scenes.body:
ClaimWright draws explicitly on Robert Pennock’s scientific-virtues work: curiosity, honesty, attention to evidence, and willingness to revise.

The engineering question is how to turn those commitments into repeatable actions—and preserve evidence that the actions happened.

A declaration states a value. A gate checks a condition. An enforcement point can stop an action.
scenes.visual:
Values → observable practice

Honesty
Expose source-access limits
Skepticism
Seek counterevidence
Humility
Retain uncertainty and revise claims
Accountability
Record who approved what
scenes.notes: This connection is especially relevant to BEACON, but it does not imply Pennock or MSU endorses these tools. The mapping is ClaimWright’s practical interpretation.

scenes.title: Write the agreement before the output.
scenes.body:
ClaimWright supplies a human-readable collaboration agreement, policy files, claim states, review roles, and pre- and post-action checks.

A claim may be exploratory, supported, contested, stale, contradicted, or private-only. The workflow makes those distinctions visible before public release.

The offline publication gate checks declared reviews, artifact and policy hashes, similarity findings, and destination requirements. A passing check does not establish scientific truth or grant permission to publish.
scenes.visual:
A claim has a history

  1. Working claim
  2. Evidence + source fit
  3. Adversarial review
  4. Release decision
  5. Correction when evidence changes
scenes.notes: The public revision includes the policy substrate checker and an offline publication gate, with 23 passing software regression tests. These tests do not authenticate a human approval or certify claim accuracy. Not every declared lifecycle state or action is automatically enforced; human publication responsibility remains explicit.

scenes.title: A gate must be able to say “stop.”
scenes.body:
GroundRecall defines policy decision points around memory operations. Its documented outcomes include allow, require review, soft gate, hard gate, and deny; hard gates and denials block covered operations.

Keep the decision to propose an action separate from the authority to execute it. Enforcement has to happen on the actual path to the protected operation.

Try this simplified release rule. Change an input and inspect the reason.

Teaching simulation · no data is submitted

Hold: resolve the citation and check claim support.
scenes.visual:
The enforcement boundary

Proposed action↓Evaluate policy↓Permit · hold · block↓Execute only if permitted

Actual protection depends on configured policy and covered call paths. This diagram is not a claim of complete enforcement.
scenes.notes: The simulation is illustrative JavaScript, not the ClaimWright or GroundRecall engine. Demonstrate that a DOI alone does not clear a publication gate. Policy evaluation alone is not enforcement; inspect which call paths actually honor its result.

scenes.title: Remember why, not just what.
scenes.body:
GroundRecall keeps durable claims, source provenance, review status, and release scope outside an individual chat. Indexed search finds candidate records; graph relations recover context.

Epistemap supplies a shared graph representation, traversal, and diagnostics. It stays below domain policy.

A retrieved record is evidence to inspect. A graph edge or confidence estimate is not a truth certificate.
scenes.visual:
An illustrative provenance graph

Source passage
supports ↓
Scoped claim
reviewed by ↓
Review receipt
challenged by ↓
Counterevidence

Search locates a record. The graph exposes its dependencies and challenges.
scenes.notes: A practical retrieval loop: search, inspect provenance and date, check the current artifact, then use the result. Graph diagnostics can expose missing evidence; they cannot make bad source material reliable. Private release tags must survive export.

scenes.title: Keep the source trail through transformation.
scenes.body:
doclift normalizes legacy Word and WordPerfect documents into text, Markdown, and structured sidecars that preserve extraction information.

Didactopus turns educational material into draft learning domains, prerequisite graphs, practice, and reviewable skill artifacts.

Conversion is a transformation to inspect. Ingestion does not automatically make material accurate, mastered, or suitable for publication.
scenes.visual:
From old files to usable structure

  1. Legacy source
  2. doclift: extraction + conversion report
  3. Didactopus: draft domain + prerequisites
  4. Review + learner evidence
  5. Learning pack or reusable skill
scenes.notes: Explain sidecars as small companion files recording structure and conversion decisions. Separate the original source from the extracted text, interpretation, and teaching artifact. A detected prerequisite still deserves review.

scenes.title: From a rough reference to a defensible citation.
scenes.body:
CiteGeist converts free-text references into draft BibTeX, resolves identifiers and metadata, retains conflicts and provenance, and expands a bibliography through citation links and topic search.

It supports directed literature discovery as well as repair of references already in hand.

Verification has two questions: Does this work exist? and Does this work support this claim?
scenes.visual:
The bibliography workbench

  1. Rough reference or research question
  2. Candidate match
  3. Identifier + metadata verification
  4. Claim-support review
  5. Reviewed BibTeX + public source link

Rejected and unresolved candidates are useful review history.
scenes.notes: CiteGeist’s README describes substantial implemented plumbing and remaining gaps in evaluation depth and researcher ergonomics. Do not collapse metadata matching, disambiguation, and reading for support into one “verified” badge.

scenes.title: A workbench became a publication pipeline.
scenes.body:
The inspected CiteGeist history begins on 19 March 2026. That is a reproducible repository milestone; the date of first personal use still needs confirmation.

By May, there were large bibliography exports and public educational artifacts. July brought further graph, governance, and publication work.

These artifacts show increased scope of work. They do not, by themselves, measure time saved or establish what would have happened without AI.
scenes.visual:
Documented milestones · 2026

19 MarCiteGeist initial commit

02 MayBibliography build snapshot

02 JulAI assurance preprint

12 JulClaimWright initial framework
scenes.notes: Invite the speaker to add the first actual CiteGeist use and the personal before/after account. Dates here are artifact evidence, not a causal study of AI productivity.

scenes.title: A bibliography people can inspect and reuse.
scenes.body:
The retained May build contains 1,029 topic pages and 39,930 citation placements, with DOI links and abstract records where available.

A direct check of the live abiogenesis page found 76 entries, expandable citation details, and BibTeX.

The accomplishment is a navigable, reusable research surface. Quality still depends on relevance checks and editorial review.
scenes.visual:
May 2026 build snapshot

1,029Topic pages
39,930Citation placements across topics

26,604 DOI placements · 17,432 abstract placements.
Counts are not deduplicated unique works or a count of individually verified claims.
scenes.notes: Open the public page if useful, but the screenshot-free presentation works offline. Explain the stale search-engine copy found during preparation: direct live checking returned the expanded page. More citations can increase review burden; volume is not the quality measure.

scenes.title: An Archive update is a coordinated process.
scenes.body:
Start with the English source: preserve attributed legacy articles, review changes, and use CiteGeist to improve the supporting bibliography. Render the changed pages and check their links and citations.

Queue new or changed content for Spanish, French, German, and Portuguese. Local LLM workers handle bulk translation; GenieHive provides a shared way to find and route to model services.

Keep translation generation, review, and publication distinct. The process connects source maintenance, reusable citations, multilingual access, and local compute.
scenes.visual:
From source change to public update

  1. Review English content + references
  2. Render and check affected pages
  3. Queue translation by page + language
  4. Run local LLMs; inspect outputs
  5. Publish a scoped update

GenieHive routes to model services; the site and queue determine the work.
scenes.notes: Explain this as the maintenance workflow used for the modernized Archive. Keep historical author text distinct from newly added study material. Translation covers four active target languages. Workers can use GenieHive or compatible endpoints directly; do not imply every job passes through the router. The deep dives cover queue recovery, the dated public translation milestone, and model hosting. No inference-cost savings or expert translation-quality rate has been measured for this talk.

scenes.title: Publish explanations with a route back to evidence.
scenes.body:
The public Notebook on Evolution presents beginner routes, concept pages, learning paths, and source-trail status.

SciSiteForge provides reusable static-site patterns and optional bridges to the ingestion, memory, learning, and bibliography tools.

Public readers need an explanation they can use and a source trail they can follow. Private working material needs a separate release decision.
scenes.visual:
Two sides of a public artifact

Reader’s surface
Concept · example · learning path
Evidence surface
Source trail · review status · bibliography
Release boundary
Reviewed material crosses; private working files stay behind
scenes.notes: This is an observed public site, not evidence of measured gains in learning. Show the beginner route to instructors and graduate students. Site frameworks can support release boundaries, but each build must still be checked.

scenes.title: Make the learning process inspectable.
scenes.body:
The Didactopus Information and Entropy example produces a topic pack, learner-session artifacts, progress views, and a reusable skill bundle.

Its skill demonstration includes an explanation, an evaluation, and a follow-up requesting a limitation or assumption.

That demonstrates the workflow. Synthetic learner scores do not demonstrate that a person learned the material.
scenes.visual:
Learning evidence loop

  1. Concept + prerequisite
  2. Independent attempt
  3. Feedback + critique
  4. New evidence of understanding
  5. Revise the next learning step

For a human study: test transfer and delayed retention, not just immediate answer quality.
scenes.notes: Useful BEACON research question: does a graph-grounded mentor improve unaided transfer compared with answer generation alone? Clearly distinguish the proposed human experiment from the included deterministic/synthetic demo.

scenes.title: Name the mechanism and its failure modes.
scenes.body:
The Mechanism-Aware AI Assurance preprint proposes an Operational Premise Taxonomy: describe the computational mechanisms a system actually uses, then examine the assumptions and failure modes that follow.

It adds a question to the governance discussion: what evidence links the stated policy to the implemented system?

This is a public, inspectable proposal. Its usefulness as an assurance method remains something to evaluate.
scenes.visual:
A question for any AI workflow

Intended behavior
What do we say it does?
Implemented mechanism
What actually produces the result?
Failure evidence
What breaks, under which conditions?
Control
What detects, contains, or corrects that failure?
scenes.notes: Use this as a conceptual bridge back to industry promises. Do not present the preprint as peer-reviewed validation. The bibliography and governed-memory tools support traceability; no controlled attribution of the paper to a particular tool is claimed.

scenes.title: The controls create work, too.
scenes.body:
A source can be wrong. A citation can match the wrong work. A graph can preserve a mistaken interpretation. A policy can be bypassed by an uncovered path.

Review takes time, and repeated model agreement can reproduce a shared error. Local processing alone does not establish privacy or correctness.

Track error rates, review effort, corrections, and boundary failures alongside the number of artifacts produced.

Read the repository capability review and alternatives feature analysis →
scenes.visual:
What to measure next

  • Citation identity accuracy
  • Claim–source fit
  • Time to find supporting evidence
  • Stale-claim detection
  • Release-boundary failures
  • Human review workload
scenes.notes: These are proposed evaluation dimensions, not a reported benchmark result for this stack. State the gap openly: much of the demonstrated progress is integration and artifact production.

scenes.title: Try a bounded, falsifiable comparison.
scenes.body:
Choose one literature question. Compare a baseline workflow with a provenance-preserving workflow on the same task and time budget.

Have reviewers evaluate citation identity, source fit, uncertainty, and time needed to audit each result. Record rejected candidates and corrections.

For teaching, add an unaided transfer task. For agents, test whether a prohibited action is actually blocked.
scenes.visual:
Suggested pilot, not a completed study

BaselineExisting practice
↔
Governed workflowExplicit evidence + review

Same task. Comparable resources. Independent review. Predeclared success and failure criteria.
scenes.notes: Ask a postdoc, instructor, and graduate student what evidence would change their practice. The proposal should be scaled to available time; a small pilot can estimate review burden before a larger study.

scenes.title: What would earn your trust?
scenes.body:
Which tasks are worth delegating now?

Which decisions should require an explicit human release?

What evidence would show that the system helps us do better science—and makes our mistakes easier to find?

Explore the eight-repository comparison, alternatives, and adoption tradeoffs.

The output is an artifact.
The responsibility stays with us.
scenes.visual:
Take this back to your lab

One task.
One boundary.
One test.

Start with something useful, reviewable, and small enough to learn from.
scenes.notes: Return to the task named at the beginning. Invite disagreement and specific failure cases. Leave the source appendix available for questions.

deep_dives.title: ClaimWright & policy gates
deep_dives.description: From an explicit agreement to a check that can stop an operation.

scenes.title: Write down what “responsible” requires.
scenes.body:
ClaimWright’s memorandum, policy files, and role cards make a collaboration agreement inspectable. They describe claim states, evidence expectations, review responsibilities, and release boundaries.

The same claim can be useful in private exploration and unready for public release. A review record should retain its scope, source access, unresolved objections, and the reason for the release decision.

The agreement supplies a standard against which to review work. The publication CLI now validates review records, binds them to artifacts and policy, and retains unresolved findings. Human release approval remains separate.
scenes.visual:
What a review should preserve

Claim
What is being asserted, and within what scope?
Evidence
Which source was actually inspected?
Decision
What remains unresolved; who approved release?
scenes.notes: Use the repository’s documented full-path example as an illustration. Do not present all declared claim states or checks as automatically enforced features.

scenes.title: Put the check on the path to the action.
scenes.body:
A policy decision point evaluates a proposed operation. An enforcement point acts on that result before the protected operation runs. Logging a rejection while still performing the action would fail this design.

GroundRecall documents allow, require-review, soft-gate, hard-gate, and deny outcomes around covered memory operations. Actual protection depends on the policy configuration and the call paths that honor it.

A useful test is behavioral: attempt a prohibited operation and check that it was blocked, with a reason that can be inspected.
scenes.visual:
Illustrative release boundary

  1. Propose a public export
  2. Check scope, evidence, and review
  3. Hold or deny when requirements fail
  4. Execute only on a permitted path

ClaimWright defines the agreement; GroundRecall implements policy hooks for its own operations.
scenes.notes: Connect back to the main talk’s teaching simulation. This is a design explanation, not a claim that every local tool or operating-system command is governed by GroundRecall.

deep_dives.title: GroundRecall & Epistemap
deep_dives.description: Find prior work, inspect its source trail, and preserve reasons to revise it.

scenes.title: Store a claim with the reasons behind it.
scenes.body:
A durable record needs more than a sentence. GroundRecall can retain concepts, claims, sources, review state, and release scope outside the chat that produced them.

Epistemap supplies common nodes and relations so projects can traverse dependencies and inspect graph structure. It does not decide what a review status means or authorize a release.

Keep the source, the interpretation, and the review decision distinguishable. That makes a later correction possible.
scenes.visual:
An illustrative record

  1. Source + access date
  2. Claim + scope
  3. Support and challenge relations
  4. Review state + release scope
scenes.notes: This is a conceptual record, not an export of private memory. Explain the separation between a document’s statement and a curator’s interpretation.

scenes.title: Search is the beginning of checking.
scenes.body:
Indexed full-text search locates candidate records. Graph traversal then exposes related sources, dependencies, challenges, and context that a phrase match alone may miss.

Preparing this presentation followed that pattern: consult prior-work records, locate the relevant repository or artifact, inspect it afresh, then choose evidence suitable for a public talk.

Durable memory saves context from being lost. Fresh inspection establishes whether that context still applies.
scenes.visual:
The retrieval loop

  1. Search a name or question
  2. Inspect record and provenance
  3. Follow relevant graph relations
  4. Check the current source artifact
  5. Use the result with its limits
scenes.notes: The preparation example describes work performed for this presentation, not a benchmark. No private records, host names, or internal endpoints are displayed.

scenes.title: A correction should reach dependent claims.
scenes.body:
If a premise becomes stale or is challenged, connected claims deserve another look. Graph dependencies help identify that review surface.

Epistemap includes temporal and contradiction diagnostics, plus assessment-readiness checks for provenance and confidence metadata. GroundRecall supplies the domain-specific review and release workflow.

A confidence estimate describes an assessment under stated assumptions. It does not turn an unsupported claim into a fact.
scenes.visual:
Questions a graph helps expose

Dependency
Which conclusions rely on this premise?
Time
Was the evidence current for this claim?
Review
What needs checking after a correction?
scenes.notes: Keep implemented diagnostics separate from a claim of automatic, comprehensive stale-claim repair. Human decisions and policy remain necessary.

deep_dives.title: doclift & Didactopus
deep_dives.description: Transform source files into reviewable learning material and reusable skills.

scenes.title: Recover structure without losing the source.
scenes.body:
doclift handles legacy Word and WordPerfect files. It emits extracted text and normalized Markdown, together with companion JSON files for conversion decisions, layout cues, tables, figures, and asset inventory.

Those companion files make extraction quality inspectable. The original and the normalized text remain distinguishable when a downstream system uses the material.

The handoff is a source bundle. It is ready for review, not automatically ready to teach or publish.
scenes.visual:
The conversion bundle

Readable text
Extracted text and normalized Markdown
Structure
Layout, table, and figure records
Audit trail
Manifest and conversion report
scenes.notes: doclift owns legacy-format normalization. Its README lists RTF, higher-fidelity DOCX, old HTML, and OCR as follow-on plans, so do not imply these are all implemented.

scenes.title: Turn content into a path through concepts.
scenes.body:
Didactopus consumes educational material and drafts domain packs: concepts, prerequisites, learning routes, attribution, and review flags. Packs pass through validation, review, and promotion.

A learning graph can help choose the next concept. Practice and learner evidence then inform the next step rather than treating a generated explanation as proof of mastery.

Ask the learner to explain, apply, and identify limitations. Keep the evidence of understanding alongside the learning path.
scenes.visual:
The learning loop

  1. Reviewed concepts + prerequisites
  2. A learner attempt
  3. Feedback and evaluation
  4. Evidence of capability
  5. An adjusted next step
scenes.notes: This is the documented workflow and a pedagogical rationale, not a demonstrated human learning effect. Mention pack, notebook, and hybrid output modes only if useful.

scenes.title: Inspect a worked example end to end.
scenes.body:
The Information and Entropy example produces a topic pack, learner-session records, progress views, and a reusable skill bundle. The skill demo includes explanation, evaluation, and a follow-up about an assumption or limitation.

A separate provider transcript illustrates how a local-LLM-backed mentor interaction can look. The deterministic demo’s synthetic learner scores demonstrate the plumbing, not a person’s learning.

For BEACON, the next evidence would be unaided transfer and delayed retention measured with real learners.
scenes.visual:
What the example makes inspectable

Domain
Concepts and their prerequisites
Session
Attempts, feedback, and evaluation
Export
Progress records and a reusable skill
scenes.notes: Offer the repository’s public example artifacts for inspection. Do not describe synthetic learner scores as Wesley’s or any human student’s performance.

deep_dives.title: CiteGeist
deep_dives.description: From rough references through verification and discovery to the TalkOrigins bibliography.

scenes.title: A citation starts as a candidate.
scenes.body:
CiteGeist can extract a rough reference from free text and turn it into draft BibTeX. Identifier lookup and title-based matching help resolve the work and enrich its metadata.

A local database retains identifiers, source provenance, review states, and field conflicts. Alternate candidates and unresolved cases remain available for inspection.

Resolve identity before accepting metadata. Read the source before treating it as support for a particular claim.
scenes.visual:
Two different checks

  1. Free-text reference
  2. Candidate works + identifiers
  3. Identity and metadata review
  4. Claim–source fit review
  5. Reviewed BibTeX export
scenes.notes: Use the two verification questions from the main section. A successful DOI lookup is evidence of identity, not necessarily of correct interpretation or relevance.

scenes.title: Use a question to grow a bibliography.
scenes.body:
A topic phrase or seed bibliography can start a bootstrap workflow. Citation links lead to related works; topic search and local text search help find candidates beyond the references already in hand.

The workbench records where candidates came from. Relevance review then separates useful additions from duplicates, ambiguous matches, and results that only share terminology.

Directed discovery is a repeatable search-and-review process. It is not evidence that the resulting bibliography is exhaustive.
scenes.visual:
From search to selection

Seed
A research question or known work
Expand
Citation links and scholarly metadata sources
Curate
Relevance, duplicates, conflicts, and source fit
scenes.notes: The repository supports citation-graph expansion and topic workflows. Avoid presenting a semantic similarity result as an argument that two papers make the same claim.

scenes.title: Repair an old bibliography; make it reusable.
scenes.body:
The TalkOrigins example handles legacy plaintext references, including repeated-author notation, and produces topic-level seed BibTeX, cleaned text, review reports, and reconstructed pages.

This became a public application: the retained May build has 1,029 topic pages and 39,930 citation placements. Readers can inspect entries, follow source links, and reuse BibTeX.

The output connects a legacy collection to continued literature discovery. Counts describe publication scope, not unique works or a measured accuracy rate.
scenes.visual:
The documented application

  1. Legacy topic bibliography
  2. Normalize references and author repeats
  3. Review parsing, duplicates, and metadata
  4. Expand and curate by topic
  5. Publish readable entries + BibTeX
scenes.notes: Connect this worked application to the main TalkOrigins outcome. Citation placements repeat works across topics. The first actual date of personal CiteGeist use still awaits speaker confirmation.

deep_dives.title: TalkOrigins updates & translation
deep_dives.description: Follow a source change through bibliography, language work, and publication.

scenes.title: Preserve the article; make additions legible.
scenes.body:
The modernization workflow preserves attributed legacy article content while changing the surrounding presentation and adding clearly separate study material, navigation, and bibliography support.

For bibliography updates, CiteGeist supplies the topic data. Pages and BibTeX exports are rendered, index entries are updated, and citation counts and links are checked.

Keep the scope of an update visible: which source changed, which generated pages follow from it, and which checks were performed.
scenes.visual:
A scoped English update

  1. Choose a page or bibliography topic
  2. Review source text and citations
  3. Render affected pages + downloads
  4. Update navigation and indexes
  5. Inspect the scoped changes
scenes.notes: Separate the historical source of record from the modernization output. This workflow description comes from inspected maintainer scripts and public artifacts; it is not a claim that every legacy statement has been newly fact-checked.

scenes.title: Translate changed content as tracked work.
scenes.body:
New and changed pages enter work orders for Spanish, French, German, and Portuguese. When only a large bibliography index’s rows or count change, the workflow can update those fragments rather than translating the entire index again.

The translator uses a terminology compendium and bounded chunks. The resilient queue checks available workers, claims a batch-and-language unit, records results, and can resume interrupted work.

Local models handle bulk work. The configured hybrid policy reserves a capped fallback for selected routes or outputs with failures or warnings.
scenes.visual:
A page × language work unit

  1. Reviewed English source
  2. Work order + terminology
  3. Bounded translation requests
  4. Output + warnings + run record
  5. Check and publish the intended files
scenes.notes: Do not imply queue completion means an expert has approved the prose. Local workers can be directly addressed or reached through GenieHive. Explain a lease as a temporary claim on a work unit that can expire after interruption.

scenes.title: Translation coverage and review are different records.
scenes.body:
The public status page’s 8 July 2026 snapshot lists 2,872 translated pages per language across Spanish, French, German, and Portuguese, with no remaining work in that recorded queue.

That is a generation milestone for a defined set of pages. SciSiteForge supports a visible automated-translation disclaimer and an automated-unreviewed label until review.

Revisit scientific terminology, negation, links, and attribution during review. Publish corrections and regenerate affected translations when the English source changes.
scenes.visual:
Keep both kinds of status

Coverage
Has an output been generated for this page and language?
Review
Has its meaning and technical wording been checked?
Currency
Does it still match the English source?

The published queue snapshot is dated; it is not a live claim about every Archive page.
scenes.notes: Figures were fetched from the public status page for this presentation. Do not convert “translated” to “expert-reviewed.” The retained evidence summary records the published timestamp and scope.

deep_dives.title: GenieHive & local LLMs
deep_dives.description: Separate model hosting, request routing, and application-level work.

scenes.title: Host the model; route the request.
scenes.body:
A model runtime loads weights and runs inference on local hardware. In this workflow, llama.cpp-based services provide local translation capacity; the inspected queue configuration selects Qwen3.5-9B workers.

GenieHive registers hosts and services, receives health and inventory updates, and routes chat, embedding, or transcription requests. A client can address a model directly or use a role such as scientific translator.

The runtime runs the model. GenieHive chooses a suitable service. The application decides what work to request.
scenes.visual:
Three responsibilities

  1. Application: translation job
  2. GenieHive: role + health-aware routing
  3. Runtime: loaded model + inference
  4. Application: output checks + review

Compatible endpoints can also be called directly; not every local job passes through GenieHive.
scenes.notes: Explain local hosting without exposing internal addresses, host inventory, or credentials. The model label is an inspected configuration, not a claim that workers are online at presentation time. GenieHive’s node agent does not start or supervise upstream model servers.

scenes.title: A steady queue makes local compute useful.
scenes.body:
Translation creates many bounded jobs with similar output requirements. The queue can assign work to available services, retain results, and retry interrupted units instead of restarting the whole collection.

GenieHive’s documented routing can consider loaded state, health, observed performance, and scheduling policy. Its translation guidance emphasizes enough context and predictable, translation-only responses.

Local hosting shifts the cost question toward hardware, electricity, utilization, maintenance, and review. Its value needs measurement alongside any reduction in paid API use.
scenes.visual:
Match the service to the work

Ready
Healthy, loaded, and enough context
Predictable
Stable response format and terminology
Recoverable
Recorded outputs and resumable queue units
scenes.notes: No cost or speed benchmark is claimed. Do not equate an endpoint responding with a high-quality scientific translation. The queue’s recovery mechanism and GenieHive’s request scheduling are separate layers.

scenes.title: Make the routing policy inspectable.
scenes.body:
The optional Foundation gateway profile adds revocable client keys, model and operation scopes, metadata-only request auditing, and opt-in token or cost budgets.

Those controls depend on configuration; the casual example leaves them disabled. Local placement alone also does not establish privacy, model quality, or complete control of an application’s actions.

For a lab deployment, specify who may call which service, what is recorded, and what happens when a limit or service failure is reached.

Versioned evaluation contracts now retain case results, dataset and evaluator identity, pass thresholds, and declared hard failures. The public starter cases test output contracts; they do not establish model quality or automatically promote a route.

Compare GenieHive with LiteLLM and GPUStack →
scenes.visual:
Questions for a local service

Access
Which client may use which operation?
Budget
What happens when a configured limit is reached?
Evidence
Can the request decision be inspected?
scenes.notes: Describe these as implemented optional capabilities in the pinned public README, not proof that every local translation worker uses the gateway profile. Connect the proposed deployment questions to the constructive adoption preface.

deep_dives.title: SciSiteForge & public artifacts
deep_dives.description: Build a reader-facing site while preserving evidence and release boundaries.

scenes.title: Give readers an explanation and a source trail.
scenes.body:
SciSiteForge supplies static-site patterns for topic pages, bibliographies, language switching, search, and Notebook learning paths. Optional bridges connect source normalization, memory, learning packs, and citation data.

The public Notebook on Evolution illustrates the reader-facing aim: beginner routes and concept pages with a path back to sources and review status.

A public export is a selected artifact. It should contain the material appropriate for readers, with provenance and uncertainty they can understand.
scenes.visual:
Three reader needs

Orientation
Where do I start, and what does this concept mean?
Evidence
Where can I check or follow up?
Status
What has been reviewed, and what remains provisional?
scenes.notes: Do not imply the static site publishes the entire private knowledge store. The public Notebook is an observed artifact; it does not demonstrate measured learning gains.

scenes.title: Make the mechanism available for criticism.
scenes.body:
The Mechanism-Aware AI Assurance preprint asks how implemented computational mechanisms relate to a system’s assumptions and failure modes. It provides a public proposal that others can inspect and challenge.

The connection to this workbench is traceability: a reader should be able to distinguish a policy statement, implemented control, demonstration, and measured result.

Public artifacts make review possible. Evidence that a method improves outcomes still requires an appropriate evaluation.
scenes.visual:
An assurance argument

Mechanism
What produces the behavior?
Assumption
What must hold for the claim to apply?
Failure test
What observation would challenge it?
scenes.notes: The preprint is not peer-reviewed validation or evidence that any individual tool caused the research result. Present it as another inspectable public output.
